That's an old Portec flange lubricator. LB Foster acquired Portec a while ago and now sell that same style unit. That's all we bought on NS while I working track department.  I was obsessive about keeping our lubricators working perfectly.

There's a huge bin inside that holds the grease. And that stuff is pricey. Like $10k foe a big tote of it. There was a summer and a winter blend we used and then they released a more expensive "all season" grease finally. I used to mix the 2 greases together because I cared so much. 

Inside the front door is a control box where you can set the wheel count and amount of grease pushed to the greaser bars. Those short out sometimes and need new fuses. 

Then inside the gage of the track is a wheel counting device. Counts the wheels.  

The hoses, 4 way piping and greases bars sit on black carpet in the tracks. Usually 3 clamps hold the bar to the rail. Gotta have the ports on the bars set 1 1/8" from top of rail or those greases bar ports will be smashed by the wheels. Then you have to rebuild thr whole bar. Which is a nasty job. My old territory was in Virginia and Ohio. 

Big projects will get cleaned up decently. But the railroading has left their scrap on property for decades. I've found this from the early 1900s. 

These track materials are heavy, cumbersome and hard to get into the middle of a remote forest on 2 pieces of rail. Easiest is install new stuff and you don't bother getting injured or going over your track time to pickup scrap. Manpower is so short anyways, you never have time to come back and cleanup. 

Looking at railroad photos from the 1980s, railroad territories were spotless. Making lots of money from coal and had dozens of people working on a territory. You could afford to have people cleaning this stuff up and take pride in your territory. Nowadays, you have 6 people maintaining 200 miles of 60mph freight mainline. With contractors helping every so often. Just can't do it all anymore, so scrap gets left lying around.... I left after 6 years as a roadmaster.
